claim: African trypanosomes evade host immune clearance by antigenic variation, causing persistent infections in humans and animals.
source: African trypanosomes evade host immune clearance by antigenic variation, causing persistent infections in humans and animals.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Trypanosomes express a homogeneous surface coat of variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs).
source: These parasites express a homogeneous surface coat of variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome biology.

claim: Trypanosomes transcribe one out of hundreds of VSG genes at a time from telomeric expression sites (ESs).
source: They transcribe one out of hundreds of VSG genes at a time from telomeric expression sites (ESs) and periodically change the VSG expressed by transcriptional switching or recombination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VSG expression in trypanosomes.

claim: Trypanosomes periodically change the VSG expressed by transcriptional switching or recombination.
source: They transcribe one out of hundreds of VSG genes at a time from telomeric expression sites (ESs) and periodically change the VSG expressed by transcriptional switching or recombination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antigenic variation mechanisms.

claim: Telomeric ES activation and silencing entail an on/off genetic switch controlled by a nuclear phosphoinositide signaling system.
source: We report that telomeric ES activation and silencing entail an on/off genetic switch controlled by a nuclear phosphoinositide signaling system.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches including RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and biochemical assays.

claim: The nuclear phosphoinositide signaling system includes a nuclear phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphatase (PIP5Pase), its substrate PI(3,4,5)P3, and the repressor-activator protein 1 (RAP1).
source: This system includes a nuclear phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphatase (PIP5Pase), its substrate PI(3,4,5)P3, and the repressor-activator protein 1 (RAP1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing interactions and functional relationships between these components.

claim: RAP1 binds to ES sequences flanking VSG genes via its DNA binding domains.
source: RAP1 binds to ES sequences flanking VSG genes via its DNA binding domains and represses VSG transcription.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing RAP1 binding to 70 bp and telomeric repeats flanking VSG genes.

claim: RAP1 represses VSG transcription.
source: RAP1 binds to ES sequences flanking VSG genes via its DNA binding domains and represses VSG transcription.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that RAP1 knockdown results in transcription of all ESs simultaneously, as cited from previous work.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 binds to the N-terminus of RAP1.
source: In contrast, PI(3,4,5)P3 binds to the N-terminus of RAP1 and controls its DNA binding activity.
evidence: This is supported by binding assays showing that rRAP1^1-300-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 controls RAP1's DNA binding activity.
source: In contrast, PI(3,4,5)P3 binds to the N-terminus of RAP1 and controls its DNA binding activity.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA and MST data showing that PI(3,4,5)P3 inhibits RAP1 binding to DNA.

claim: Transient inactivation of PIP5Pase results in the accumulation of nuclear PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: Transient inactivation of PIP5Pase results in the accumulation of nuclear PI(3,4,5)P3, which binds RAP1 and displaces it from ESs, activating transcription of silent ESs and VSG switching.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased PI(3,4,5)P3 associated with RAP1-HA in cells expressing mutant PIP5Pase.

claim: Accumulated PI(3,4,5)P3 binds RAP1 and displaces it from ESs.
source: Transient inactivation of PIP5Pase results in the accumulation of nuclear PI(3,4,5)P3, which binds RAP1 and displaces it from ESs, activating transcription of silent ESs and VSG switching.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing loss of RAP1 binding to ESs in cells expressing mutant PIP5Pase.

claim: Displacement of RAP1 from ESs activates transcription of silent ESs and VSG switching.
source: Transient inactivation of PIP5Pase results in the accumulation of nuclear PI(3,4,5)P3, which binds RAP1 and displaces it from ESs, activating transcription of silent ESs and VSG switching.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq showing upregulation of silent ES VSG genes and VSG-seq showing VSG switching after PIP5Pase inactivation.

claim: The phosphoinositide signaling system is required for the developmental silencing of VSG genes.
source: The system is also required for the developmental silencing of VSG genes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing upregulation of ES VSG genes in procyclic forms after PIP5Pase knockdown.

claim: T. brucei have over 2500 VSG genes and pseudogenes, primarily on subtelomeres.
source: T. brucei have over 2500 VSG genes and pseudogenes, primarily on subtelomeres, and ~20 telomeric expression sites (ESs), each containing a VSG gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the T. brucei genome.

claim: T. brucei have approximately 20 telomeric expression sites (ESs), each containing a VSG gene.
source: T. brucei have over 2500 VSG genes and pseudogenes, primarily on subtelomeres, and ~20 telomeric expression sites (ESs), each containing a VSG gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. brucei genome organization.

claim: Only one VSG gene is transcribed at a time from a telomeric ES.
source: Only one VSG gene is transcribed at a time from a telomeric ES.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VSG monogenic expression.

claim: Antigenic variation occurs via transcriptional switching between ESs or VSG gene recombination within ESs.
source: Antigenic variation occurs via transcriptional switching between ESs or VSG gene recombination within ESs (Cestari and Stuart, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active VSG gene is developmentally regulated.
source: The active VSG gene is developmentally regulated, and its expression is silenced in parasites encountered in the tsetse fly vector, for example procyclic and epimastigote forms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VSG expression during the trypanosome life cycle.

claim: VSG expression is silenced in procyclic and epimastigote forms.
source: The active VSG gene is developmentally regulated, and its expression is silenced in parasites encountered in the tsetse fly vector, for example procyclic and epimastigote forms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about developmental regulation of VSG expression.

claim: Epimastigotes develop into transmissible metacyclic trypomastigotes, which re-activate VSG gene expression before infecting mammals.
source: Epimastigotes develop into transmissible metacyclic trypomastigotes, which re-activate VSG gene expression before infecting mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the trypanosome life cycle.

claim: Expression of mutant PIP5Pase resulted in 1807 genes upregulated and 33 downregulated.
source: The expression of the Mut PIP5Pase resulted in 1807 genes upregulated and 33 downregulated (Figure 1B,≥2 fold change, p-value ≤0.01, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: All silent ES VSG genes were upregulated upon expression of mutant PIP5Pase.
source: Notably, all silent ES VSG genes were upregulated (Figure 1B, C), consistent with their transcription.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: There was a ~10-fold decrease in the active VSG (VSG2) and ESAG mRNAs upon expression of mutant PIP5Pase.
source: In contrast, there was a~10-fold decrease in the active VSG (VSG2) and ESAG mRNAs (Figure 1B, C), implying decreased expression of the active ES (BES1) genes, perhaps resulting from competition among ESs for polymerase or factors required for their transcription.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The decreased expression of active ES genes may result from competition among ESs for polymerase or factors required for their transcription.
source: In contrast, there was a~10-fold decrease in the active VSG (VSG2) and ESAG mRNAs (Figure 1B, C), implying decreased expression of the active ES (BES1) genes, perhaps resulting from competition among ESs for polymerase or factors required for their transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claim: Upregulated genes upon mutant PIP5Pase expression were primarily from silent subtelomeric arrays, largely VSG genes and pseudogenes.
source: The remaining upregulated genes were primarily from silent subtelomeric arrays, largely VSG genes and pseudogenes (Figure 1B and D), indicating that PIP5Pase activity is also required for subtelomeric ES repression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: PIP5Pase activity is required for subtelomeric ES repression.
source: The remaining upregulated genes were primarily from silent subtelomeric arrays, largely VSG genes and pseudogenes (Figure 1B and D), indicating that PIP5Pase activity is also required for subtelomeric ES repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that subtelomeric VSG genes are upregulated when PIP5Pase is mutated.

claim: Other upregulated genes upon mutant PIP5Pase expression included primarily retrotransposons, endonucleases, and RNA polymerases.
source: Other upregulated genes included primarily retrotransposons, endonucleases, and RNA polymerases, but most chromosome core genes (Pol II and Pol III transcribed genes) were not significantly affected (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most chromosome core genes (Pol II and Pol III transcribed genes) were not significantly affected by mutant PIP5Pase expression.
source: Other upregulated genes included primarily retrotransposons, endonucleases, and RNA polymerases, but most chromosome core genes (Pol II and Pol III transcribed genes) were not significantly affected (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Re-establishing expression of WT PIP5Pase for 60 hr after its 24 hr withdrawal restored VSG monogenic expression.
source: Re-establishing expression of WT PIP5Pase for 60 hr after its 24 hr withdrawal restored VSG monogenic expression.
evidence: This is supported by VSG-seq data showing expression of specific VSGs after PIP5Pase restoration.

claim: Analysis of the population after PIP5Pase restoration revealed the expression of several VSGs other than the initially expressed VSG2, indicating a switch in VSG expression.
source: However, analysis of this population by VSG-seq revealed the expression of several VSGs other than the initially expressed VSG2 indicating a switch in VSG expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by VSG-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only a few VSGs were detected in cells expressing WT PIP5Pase by VSG-seq.
source: In contrast, only a few VSGs were detected in cells expressing WT PIP5Pase by VSG-seq (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by VSG-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: VSG switching occurred in 93 out of 94 (99%) analyzed clones after temporary PIP5Pase knockdown.
source: Analysis of isolated clones after temporary PIP5Pase knockdown (Tet -/+) confirmed VSG switching in 93 out of 94 (99%) analyzed clones (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by clonal VSG-seq data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells switched to express VSGs from silent ESs or subtelomeric regions after PIP5Pase knockdown.
source: The cells switched to express VSGs from silent ESs or subtelomeric regions, indicating switching by transcription or recombination mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by clonal VSG-seq data showing expression of different VSGs.

claim: No switching was detected in 118 isolated clones from cells continuously expressing WT PIP5Pase.
source: Moreover, no switching was detected in 118 isolated clones from cells continuously expressing WT PIP5Pase (Tet +, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by clonal VSG-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PIP5Pase activity can control the transcription and switching of VSGs.
source: The data imply that PIP5Pase activity can control the transcription and switching of VSGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing VSG switching upon PIP5Pase inactivation.

claim: PIP5Pase-V5 proteins were eliminated 72 hr after knockdown in procyclic forms.
source: Western analysis showed that PIP5Pase-V5 proteins were eliminated 72 hr after knockdown (Figure 1G), and growth arrest was detected after 5 days of knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Growth arrest was detected after 5 days of PIP5Pase knockdown in procyclic forms.
source: Western analysis showed that PIP5Pase-V5 proteins were eliminated 72 hr after knockdown (Figure 1G), and growth arrest was detected after 5 days of knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gene expression analysis showed a 5–15 log2-fold upregulation of all ES VSG genes at 72 hr after PIP5Pase knockdown in procyclic forms.
source: Gene expression analysis showed a 5–15 log2-fold upregulation of all ES VSG genes at 72 hr (Figure 1H) at a time when cells are viable and dividing.
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: VSG switching and developmental silencing depend on PIP5Pase activity.
source: The data indicate that VSG switching and developmental silencing depend on PIP5Pase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing VSG upregulation in both bloodstream and procyclic forms upon PIP5Pase inactivation.

claim: RAP1 binds telomeric or 70 bp repeats.
source: We showed that RAP1 binds telomeric or 70 bp repeats (Cestari et al., 2019), but it is unknown if it binds to other ES sequences or genomic loci.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1-HA binds primarily to silent ESs at the 70 bp and telomeric repeats.
source: We found that RAP1-HA binds primarily to silent ESs at the 70 bp and telomeric repeats, which are sequences upstream and downstream of the VSG genes in bloodstream-form ESs, respectively (Figure 2A–B and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; p-values<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A-B, E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 70 bp repeats are sequences upstream of VSG genes in bloodstream-form ESs.
source: We found that RAP1-HA binds primarily to silent ESs at the 70 bp and telomeric repeats, which are sequences upstream and downstream of the VSG genes in bloodstream-form ESs, respectively (Figure 2A–B and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; p-values<10–4).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ES structure.

claim: Telomeric repeats are sequences downstream of VSG genes in bloodstream-form ESs.
source: We found that RAP1-HA binds primarily to silent ESs at the 70 bp and telomeric repeats, which are sequences upstream and downstream of the VSG genes in bloodstream-form ESs, respectively (Figure 2A–B and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; p-values<10–4).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ES structure.

claim: There was a slight enrichment of RAP1-HA in the 50 bp repeat sequences preceding the ES promoters.
source: There was also a slight enrichment of RAP1-HA in the 50 bp repeat sequences preceding the ES promoters (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; p-values <10–4).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RAP1-HA did not bind significantly to genes, including VSG genes or pseudogenes in the ESs or subtelomeric regions.
source: However, RAP1-HA did not bind significantly to genes, including VSG genes or pseudogenes in the ESs or subtelomeric regions (Figure 2A–B and F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A-B and F.

claim: RAP1-HA was depleted from the active ES.
source: Notably, analysis of uniquely mapped reads showed that RAP1-HA was depleted from the active ES (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with RAP1 having a repressive function.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RAP1-HA depletion from the active ES is consistent with RAP1 having a repressive function.
source: Notably, analysis of uniquely mapped reads showed that RAP1-HA was depleted from the active ES (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with RAP1 having a repressive function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RAP1 is absent from the transcriptionally active ES.

claim: RAP1-HA bound sequences are rich in TAAs and GTs, including the 70 bp (TTA)7(GT/A)9 and telomeric (TTAGGG)n repeats.
source: The RAP1-HA bound sequences are rich in TAAs and GTs, including the 70 bp (TTA)7(GT/A)9 and telomeric (TTAGGG)n repeats (Figure 2A), but also T and G/T-rich sequences downstream of VSG genes.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of RAP1-HA binding sites shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RAP1-HA bound to metacyclic ESs at AT/GC-rich or (TAACCC)n repeat sequences near VSG genes.
source: RAP1-HA was also bound to metacyclic ESs at AT/GC-rich or (TAACCC)n repeat sequences near VSG genes (Figure 2E p-values < 10–4, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: RAP1-HA bound sparsely to subtelomeric regions, including centromeres.
source: RAP1-HA also bound sparsely to subtelomeric regions, including centromeres (Figure 2F p-values < 10–4), which are AT-rich in trypanosomes (Obado et al., 2007), and some binding sites overlapped with the centromeric protein kinetoplastid kinetochore 2 (KKT2) (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Centromeres are AT-rich in trypanosomes.
source: RAP1-HA also bound sparsely to subtelomeric regions, including centromeres (Figure 2F p-values < 10–4), which are AT-rich in trypanosomes (Obado et al., 2007), and some binding sites overlapped with the centromeric protein kinetoplastid kinetochore 2 (KKT2) (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Some RAP1-HA binding sites overlapped with the centromeric protein kinetoplastid kinetochore 2 (KKT2).
source: RAP1-HA also bound sparsely to subtelomeric regions, including centromeres (Figure 2F p-values < 10–4), which are AT-rich in trypanosomes (Obado et al., 2007), and some binding sites overlapped with the centromeric protein kinetoplastid kinetochore 2 (KKT2) (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published KKT2 ChIP-seq data.

claim: RAP1-HA binds primarily to telomeric and 70 bp repeats within silent ESs.
source: Hence, RAP1-HA binds primarily to telomeric and 70 bp repeats within silent ESs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ChIP-seq data.

claim: The 70 bp repeats are ES-specific sites for RAP1 binding near silent VSG genes.
source: The 70 bp repeats are ES-specific sites for RAP1 binding near silent VSG genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing RAP1 binding to 70 bp repeats in silent ESs.

claim: rRAP1-His bound to telomeric and 70 bp repeats but not to the scrambled DNA sequence.
source: rRAP1-His bound to telomeric and 70 bp repeats but not to the scrambled DNA sequence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: rRAP1-His has a Kd of 24.1 nM for telomeric repeats.
source: The MST analysis revealed a Kd of 24.1 and 10 nM of rRAP1-His for telomeric and 70 bp repeats, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by MST binding kinetics data shown in Table 1.

claim: rRAP1-His has a Kd of 10 nM for 70 bp repeats.
source: The MST analysis revealed a Kd of 24.1 and 10 nM of rRAP1-His for telomeric and 70 bp repeats, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by MST binding kinetics data shown in Table 1.

claim: RAP1 has two DNA binding domains, a central Myb (position E426-Q500) and a C-terminal Myb-like (MybL, position E639-R761) domain.
source: RAP1 has two DNA binding domains, a central Myb (position E426-Q500) and a C-terminal Myb-like (MybL, position E639-R761) domain (Figure 3A), and a divergent BRCT domain (S198-P385) (Yang et al., 2009), which is involved in RAP1 self-interaction (Afrin et al., 2020b) and perhaps other protein interactions (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and domain analysis.

claim: RAP1 has a divergent BRCT domain (S198-P385).
source: RAP1 has two DNA binding domains, a central Myb (position E426-Q500) and a C-terminal Myb-like (MybL, position E639-R761) domain (Figure 3A), and a divergent BRCT domain (S198-P385) (Yang et al., 2009), which is involved in RAP1 self-interaction (Afrin et al., 2020b) and perhaps other protein interactions (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The BRCT domain is involved in RAP1 self-interaction.
source: RAP1 has two DNA binding domains, a central Myb (position E426-Q500) and a C-terminal Myb-like (MybL, position E639-R761) domain (Figure 3A), and a divergent BRCT domain (S198-P385) (Yang et al., 2009), which is involved in RAP1 self-interaction (Afrin et al., 2020b) and perhaps other protein interactions (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The BRCT domain may be involved in other protein interactions.
source: RAP1 has two DNA binding domains, a central Myb (position E426-Q500) and a C-terminal Myb-like (MybL, position E639-R761) domain (Figure 3A), and a divergent BRCT domain (S198-P385) (Yang et al., 2009), which is involved in RAP1 self-interaction (Afrin et al., 2020b) and perhaps other protein interactions (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on citations to previous work.

claim: Both rRAP1^301-560-His and rRAP1^561-855-His proteins bound to telomeric or 70 bp repeats.
source: Both rRAP1301-560-His and rRAP1561-855-His proteins bound to telomeric or 70 bp repeats (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but no DNA binding was detected with the N-terminal rRAP11-300-His (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No DNA binding was detected with the N-terminal rRAP1^1-300-His.
source: Both rRAP1301-560-His and rRAP1561-855-His proteins bound to telomeric or 70 bp repeats (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but no DNA binding was detected with the N-terminal rRAP11-300-His (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Both Myb and MybL can independently and directly bind to 70 bp and telomeric repeats.
source: Our data show that both Myb and MybL can independently and directly bind to 70 bp and telomeric repeats.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EMSA data showing binding of both RAP1 fragments to DNA.

claim: The N-terminus of RAP1 contains a villin headpiece (VHP) domain (position Y59 to F94).
source: We found in the N-terminus of RAP1 a villin headpiece (VHP) domain (Figure 3A, position Y59 to F94, e-value <10–4), which is typically present in Villin proteins and binds phosphoinositides (Kumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by domain analysis and citation to previous work on VHP domains.

claim: VHP domains are typically present in Villin proteins and bind phosphoinositides.
source: We found in the N-terminus of RAP1 a villin headpiece (VHP) domain (Figure 3A, position Y59 to F94, e-value <10–4), which is typically present in Villin proteins and binds phosphoinositides (Kumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: T. brucei RAP1 VHP domain is conserved (~27% aa identity) with other VHPs in Villin proteins.
source: T. brucei RAP1 VHP domain is conserved (~27% aa identity) with other VHPs in Villin proteins forming a three helices fold over a hydrophobic core (Chiu et al., 2005; Meng and McKnight, 2009; Figure 4A), which is essential for phosphoinositide binding (Kumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural modeling shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The three helices fold over a hydrophobic core in VHP domains is essential for phosphoinositide binding.
source: T. brucei RAP1 VHP domain is conserved (~27% aa identity) with other VHPs in Villin proteins forming a three helices fold over a hydrophobic core (Chiu et al., 2005; Meng and McKnight, 2009; Figure 4A), which is essential for phosphoinositide binding (Kumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: rRAP1-His binds specifically to PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: We performed binding assays with rRAP1-His and biotinylated phosphoinositides (Cestari, 2019) and confirmed that rRAP1-His binds specifically to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: rRAP1^1-300-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: Moreover, we found that rRAP11-300-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 4B), but not other phosphoinositides or inositol phosphates tested (Figure 4C) and the binding was competed by a molar excess of unlabelled PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: rRAP1^1-300-His does not bind to other phosphoinositides or inositol phosphates tested.
source: Moreover, we found that rRAP11-300-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 4B), but not other phosphoinositides or inositol phosphates tested (Figure 4C) and the binding was competed by a molar excess of unlabelled PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The binding of rRAP1^1-300-His to PI(3,4,5)P3 was competed by a molar excess of unlabelled PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: Moreover, we found that rRAP11-300-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 4B), but not other phosphoinositides or inositol phosphates tested (Figure 4C) and the binding was competed by a molar excess of unlabelled PI(3,4,5)P3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by competition binding assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No PI(3,4,5)P3 binding was detected with rRAP1^301-560-His or rRAP1^561-855-His proteins.
source: However, no PI(3,4,5)P3 binding was detected with rRAP1301-560-His or rRAP1561-855-His proteins, indicating that RAP1 binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 via its N-terminus containing the VHP domain.
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data.

claim: RAP1 binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 via its N-terminus containing the VHP domain.
source: However, no PI(3,4,5)P3 binding was detected with rRAP1301-560-His or rRAP1561-855-His proteins, indicating that RAP1 binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 via its N-terminus containing the VHP domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only the N-terminal fragment binds PI(3,4,5)P3.

claim: rRAP1-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 with a Kd of 19.7 µM.
source: Moreover, binding kinetics by differential scanning fluorescence with unlabelled phosphoinositides showed that rRAP1-His binds to PI(3,4,5)P3 with a Kd of 19.7 µM (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential scanning fluorimetry data shown in Figure 4E and Table 1.

claim: There were ~100 fold more PI(3,4,5)P3 associated with RAP1-HA in cells expressing the Mut than the WT PIP5Pase.
source: There were ~100 fold more PI(3,4,5)P3 associated with RAP1-HA in cells expressing the Mut than the WT PIP5Pase (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PI(3,4,5)P3 quantification data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a mild but not significant difference in the total cellular PI(3,4,5)P3 levels comparing cells expressing WT versus Mut PIP5Pase.
source: In contrast, there was a mild but not significant difference in the total cellular PI(3,4,5)P3 levels comparing cells expressing WT versus Mut PIP5Pase (Figure 4F), implying that PIP5Pase activity controls a localized pool of PI(3,4,5)P3 in the nucleus available for RAP1 binding.
evidence: This is supported by PI(3,4,5)P3 quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PIP5Pase activity controls a localized pool of PI(3,4,5)P3 in the nucleus available for RAP1 binding.
source: In contrast, there was a mild but not significant difference in the total cellular PI(3,4,5)P3 levels comparing cells expressing WT versus Mut PIP5Pase (Figure 4F), implying that PIP5Pase activity controls a localized pool of PI(3,4,5)P3 in the nucleus available for RAP1 binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RAP1-bound PI(3,4,5)P3 increases dramatically while total cellular PI(3,4,5)P3 does not change significantly.

claim: RAP1 binds specifically to PI(3,4,5)P3 via its N-terminus in a PIP5Pase activity-dependent fashion.
source: Hence, RAP1 binds specifically to PI(3,4,5)P3 via its N-terminus in a PIP5Pase activity-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the binding assay and quantification data.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 inhibited rRAP1-His binding to telomeric repeats in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: We performed EMSA binding assays and found that PI(3,4,5)P3 inhibited rRAP1-His binding to telomeric repeats in a dose-dependent fashion, but no inhibition was detected with PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: No inhibition of rRAP1-His binding to telomeric repeats was detected with PI(4,5)P2.
source: We performed EMSA binding assays and found that PI(3,4,5)P3 inhibited rRAP1-His binding to telomeric repeats in a dose-dependent fashion, but no inhibition was detected with PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Similar PI(3,4,5)P3 binding inhibition of rRAP1-His was observed for 70 bp repeats.
source: Similar PI(3,4,5)P3 binding inhibition of rRAP1-His was observed for 70 bp repeats (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 30 µM of PI(3,4,5)P3 increased rRAP1-His Kd to telomeric repeats by ~6.5-fold.
source: Moreover, MST binding kinetics with 30 µM of PI(3,4,5)P3 increased rRAP1-His Kd to telomeric and 70 bp repeats in ~6.5-fold and ~18.5-fold, respectively (Figure 5C, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by MST binding kinetics data shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: 30 µM of PI(3,4,5)P3 increased rRAP1-His Kd to 70 bp repeats by ~18.5-fold.
source: Moreover, MST binding kinetics with 30 µM of PI(3,4,5)P3 increased rRAP1-His Kd to telomeric and 70 bp repeats in ~6.5-fold and ~18.5-fold, respectively (Figure 5C, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by MST binding kinetics data shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 did not affect rRAP1^301-560-His or rRAP1^561-855-His binding to telomeric or 70 bp repeats.
source: Notably, PI(3,4,5)P3 did not affect rRAP1301-560-His or rRAP1561-855-His binding to telomeric or 70 bp repeats (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), implying that PI(3,4,5)P3 does not compete with Myb or MybL domains direct binding to DNA.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 does not compete with Myb or MybL domains direct binding to DNA.
source: Notably, PI(3,4,5)P3 did not affect rRAP1301-560-His or rRAP1561-855-His binding to telomeric or 70 bp repeats (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), implying that PI(3,4,5)P3 does not compete with Myb or MybL domains direct binding to DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PI(3,4,5)P3 does not affect binding of RAP1 fragments containing only the DNA binding domains.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 inhibition of RAP1-DNA binding might be due to its association with RAP1 N-terminus causing conformational changes that affect Myb and MybL domains association with DNA.
source: PI(3,4,5)P3 inhibition of RAP1-DNA binding might be due to its association with RAP1 N-terminus causing conformational changes that affect Myb and MybL domains association with DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The expression of Mut PIP5Pase abolished RAP1-HA binding to 70 bp, 50 bp, and telomeric repeats in all bloodstream and metacyclic ESs.
source: The expression of Mut PIP5Pase abolished RAP1-HA binding to 70 bp, 50 bp, and telomeric repeats in all bloodstream and metacyclic ESs (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: The decreased RAP1-HA binding to ESs correlates with increased expression of VSGs and ESAG genes.
source: Notably, the decreased RAP1-HA binding to ESs correlates with increased expression of VSGs and ESAG genes (Figure 5D–E, RNAseq), indicating that PIP5Pase controls RAP1 binding to ESs and thus VSG gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by combined ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: PIP5Pase controls RAP1 binding to ESs and thus VSG gene expression.
source: Notably, the decreased RAP1-HA binding to ESs correlates with increased expression of VSGs and ESAG genes (Figure 5D–E, RNAseq), indicating that PIP5Pase controls RAP1 binding to ESs and thus VSG gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between RAP1 binding and VSG expression.

claim: The increased level of VSG and ESAG mRNAs detected in cells expressing Mut PIP5Pase may reflect increased Pol I transcription.
source: The increased level of VSG and ESAG mRNAs detected in cells expressing Mut PIP5Pase (Figure 5D) may reflect increased Pol I transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The low levels of RAP1-HA at the 50 bp repeats may affect Pol I accessibility to the BES promoter.
source: It is possible that the low levels of RAP1-HA at the 50 bp repeats affect Pol I accessibility to the BES promoter; alternatively, RAP1 association to telomeric or 70 bp repeats may affect chromatin compaction or folding impairing VSG and ESAG genes transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: RAP1 association to telomeric or 70 bp repeats may affect chromatin compaction or folding impairing VSG and ESAG genes transcription.
source: It is possible that the low levels of RAP1-HA at the 50 bp repeats affect Pol I accessibility to the BES promoter; alternatively, RAP1 association to telomeric or 70 bp repeats may affect chromatin compaction or folding impairing VSG and ESAG genes transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The expression of Mut PIP5Pase removed RAP1-HA peaks in subtelomeric regions.
source: The expression of Mut PIP5Pase also removed RAP1-HA peaks in subtelomeric regions (Figure 2F), which might impact subtelomeric chromatin organization and thus VSG expression and recombination (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Removal of RAP1-HA from subtelomeric regions might impact subtelomeric chromatin organization and thus VSG expression and recombination.
source: The expression of Mut PIP5Pase also removed RAP1-HA peaks in subtelomeric regions (Figure 2F), which might impact subtelomeric chromatin organization and thus VSG expression and recombination (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: RAP1 interacts with PIP5Pase within a 0.9 MDa complex.
source: We showed that RAP1 interacts with PIP5Pase within a 0.9 MDa complex, and this association is stable in cells expressing the Mut PIP5Pase (Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The association between RAP1 and PIP5Pase is stable in cells expressing the Mut PIP5Pase.
source: We showed that RAP1 interacts with PIP5Pase within a 0.9 MDa complex, and this association is stable in cells expressing the Mut PIP5Pase (Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 dissociation from ESs is unlikely the result of PIP5Pase mutations affecting the complex integrity.
source: Hence, RAP1 dissociation from ESs is unlikely the result of PIP5Pase mutations affecting the complex integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the RAP1-PIP5Pase complex remains stable with mutant PIP5Pase.

claim: PIP5Pase activity regulates RAP1 binding to DNA via PI(3,4,5)P3, thus controlling the reversible silencing of telomeric VSG genes.
source: Our data indicate that PIP5Pase activity regulates RAP1 binding to DNA via PI(3,4,5)P3, thus controlling the reversible silencing of telomeric VSG genes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: The reversible silencing of telomeric VSG genes in T. brucei is controlled by a phosphoinositide regulatory system.
source: We found that the reversible silencing of telomeric VSG genes in T. brucei is controlled by a phosphoinositide regulatory system.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The phosphoinositide regulatory system operates via PI(3,4,5)P3 regulation of RAP1-DNA binding and is controlled by PIP5Pase enzymatic activity.
source: The system operates via PI(3,4,5)P3 regulation of RAP1-DNA binding and is controlled by PIP5Pase enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism supported by the experimental data.

claim: The phosphoinositide regulatory system functions as an on/off genetic switch to control telomeric ES activation and silencing.
source: The system functions as an on/off genetic switch to control telomeric ES activation and silencing and indicates a mechanism to control the periodic switching of VSG genes during antigenic variation and VSG developmental silencing.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: The phosphoinositide regulatory system indicates a mechanism to control the periodic switching of VSG genes during antigenic variation and VSG developmental silencing.
source: The system functions as an on/off genetic switch to control telomeric ES activation and silencing and indicates a mechanism to control the periodic switching of VSG genes during antigenic variation and VSG developmental silencing.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The regulation requires PIP5Pase activity for continuous ES repression via dephosphorylation of PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: The regulation requires PIP5Pase activity for continuous ES repression via dephosphorylation of PI(3,4,5)P3.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism supported by the experimental data.

claim: PIP5Pase temporary inactivation results in the accumulation of PI(3,4,5)P3 bound to the RAP1 N-terminus.
source: PIP5Pase temporary inactivation results in the accumulation of PI(3,4,5)P3 bound to the RAP1 N-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by the PI(3,4,5)P3 quantification data.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 binding to RAP1 displaces RAP1 Myb and MybL domains from DNA, likely due to RAP1 conformational changes.
source: This binding displaces RAP1 Myb and MybL domains from DNA, likely due to RAP1 conformational changes, allowing polymerase elongation through the VSG gene.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the binding data and ChIP-seq results.

claim: Displacement of RAP1 from DNA allows polymerase elongation through the VSG gene.
source: This binding displaces RAP1 Myb and MybL domains from DNA, likely due to RAP1 conformational changes, allowing polymerase elongation through the VSG gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RAP1 removal correlates with increased VSG transcription.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 acts as a typical allosteric regulator controlling RAP1-DNA interactions and VSG transcriptional repression.
source: PI(3,4,5)P3 acts as a typical allosteric regulator controlling RAP1-DNA interactions and, thus, VSG transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the mechanism based on the binding data.

claim: Regulation of PIP5Pase activity and PI(3,4,5)P3 levels play a role in VSG switching.
source: Our data indicate that regulation of PIP5Pase activity and PI(3,4,5)P3 levels play a role in VSG switching.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the VSG switching data.

claim: Other phosphoinositide enzymes such as PIP5K or PLC, which act on PI(3,4,5)P3 precursors, also affect VSG expression and switching.
source: Other phosphoinositide enzymes such as PIP5K or PLC, which act on PI(3,4,5)P3 precursors, also affect VSG expression and switching (Cestari and Stuart, 2015), arguing that this system is part of a cell-wide signaling network and includes the transcriptional and recombination machinery.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The phosphoinositide signaling system is part of a cell-wide signaling network and includes the transcriptional and recombination machinery.
source: Other phosphoinositide enzymes such as PIP5K or PLC, which act on PI(3,4,5)P3 precursors, also affect VSG expression and switching (Cestari and Stuart, 2015), arguing that this system is part of a cell-wide signaling network and includes the transcriptional and recombination machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple phosphoinositide enzymes affect VSG expression.

claim: Disrupting PIP5Pase activity affects RAP1 association with subtelomeric regions and might impact long-range chromatin interactions.
source: Disrupting PIP5Pase activity affects RAP1 association with those regions and, thus, might impact long-range chromatin interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the ChIP-seq data and knowledge of chromatin organization.

claim: Subtelomeric regions and centromeres have a high frequency of interactions forming the boundaries of genome compartments in T. brucei.
source: Chromatin conformational capture analysis showed that subtelomeric regions and centromeres (many subtelomeric in T. brucei) have a high frequency of interactions forming the boundaries of genome compartments in T. brucei (Müller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chromatin organization may explain RAP1's role in VSG recombinational switching.
source: This organization may explain RAP1's role in VSG recombinational switching (Nanavaty et al., 2017) and the transcription of subtelomeric VSGs upon PIP5Pase mutation, RAP1 (Afrin et al., 2020a) or NUP1 knockdowns (DuBois et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking chromatin organization to VSG switching mechanisms.

claim: RAP1 and PIP5Pase interact and localize near the nuclear periphery.
source: RAP1 and PIP5Pase interact and localize near the nuclear periphery (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 associates with NUP1.
source: RAP1 also associates with NUP1 (Cestari et al., 2019), which knockdown derepresses silent VSG genes (DuBois et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: NUP1 knockdown derepresses silent VSG genes.
source: RAP1 also associates with NUP1 (Cestari et al., 2019), which knockdown derepresses silent VSG genes (DuBois et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 and other phosphoinositides are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi.
source: PI(3,4,5)P3 and other phosphoinositides are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi (Martin and Smith, 2006; Kim et al., 2011) and distributed to organelles, including the nuclear membrane (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphoinositides are distributed to organelles, including the nuclear membrane.
source: PI(3,4,5)P3 and other phosphoinositides are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi (Martin and Smith, 2006; Kim et al., 2011) and distributed to organelles, including the nuclear membrane (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 associates with silent telomeric ESs and lamina proteins at the nuclear periphery.
source: The scenario suggests a model in which RAP1 associates with silent telomeric ESs and lamina proteins at the nuclear periphery (Müller et al., 2018; Cestari and Stuart, 2015; DuBois et al., 2012), where regulation of silencing and activation might occur.
evidence: This is a model based on integration of current findings with previous work.

claim: The compartmentalization of silent ESs near the nuclear lamina may prevent the association of factors required for ES transcription.
source: The compartmentalization of silent ESs near the nuclear lamina may prevent the association of factors required for ES transcription, including chromatin-associated proteins and RNA processing factors.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the localization data.

claim: The active ES is depleted of RAP1.
source: In contrast, the active ES is depleted of RAP1, a process that might involve ES mRNAs competition for RAP1 binding to ES DNA (Gaurav et al., 2023), and it is enriched in proteins that facilitate transcription, including VEX2 and ESB1 (Faria et al., 2019; López-Escobar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing RAP1 depletion from the active ES.

claim: RAP1 depletion from the active ES might involve ES mRNAs competition for RAP1 binding to ES DNA.
source: In contrast, the active ES is depleted of RAP1, a process that might involve ES mRNAs competition for RAP1 binding to ES DNA (Gaurav et al., 2023), and it is enriched in proteins that facilitate transcription, including VEX2 and ESB1 (Faria et al., 2019; López-Escobar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active ES is enriched in proteins that facilitate transcription, including VEX2 and ESB1.
source: In contrast, the active ES is depleted of RAP1, a process that might involve ES mRNAs competition for RAP1 binding to ES DNA (Gaurav et al., 2023), and it is enriched in proteins that facilitate transcription, including VEX2 and ESB1 (Faria et al., 2019; López-Escobar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active ES localizes in a compartment that favours efficient processing of VSG mRNAs.
source: Furthermore, the active ES localizes in a compartment that favours efficient processing of VSG mRNAs (Faria et al., 2021; Budzak et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active and silent ESs occupy distinct subnuclear compartments and have specific associated proteins.
source: Hence, the active and silent ESs seem to occupy distinct subnuclear compartments and have specific associated proteins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data and cited literature.

claim: VSG switching may entail the inactivation of PIP5Pase, leading to reorganization of silent ES chromatin.
source: Within this model, VSG switching may entail the inactivation of PIP5Pase, leading to reorganization of silent ES chromatin, for example RAP1 removal from ESs, ESs relocation away from the nuclear lamina, and perhaps changes in ES three-dimensional organization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Once RAP1 is dissociated from ESs, other factors, such as ESB1 and VEX2, may associate with the silent ESs to initiate transcription.
source: Once RAP1 is dissociated from ESs, other factors, such as ESB1 and VEX2, may associate with the silent ESs to initiate transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on knowledge of factors required for ES transcription.

claim: The requirements for establishing VSG monogenic expression are unknown.
source: Although the requirements for establishing VSG monogenic expression are unknown, it may entail the successful association of factors with ESs for their transcription or recruitment to the ESB (Navarro and Gull, 2001; Faria et al., 2021).
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge while providing a speculative hypothesis.

claim: It is unknown if the phosphoinositide signaling system regulates antigenic variation in vivo.
source: It is unknown if this signaling system regulates antigenic variation in vivo.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: Trypanosomes may have evolved a sophisticated mechanism to regulate antigenic variation that entails genetic and signaling processes.
source: Nevertheless, the data indicate that trypanosomes may have evolved a sophisticated mechanism to regulate antigenic variation that entails genetic and signaling processes, and such processes may be conserved in other pathogens that rely on antigenic variation for infection, for example Plasmodium and Giardia, broadening opportunities for drug discovery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The antigenic variation mechanism may be conserved in other pathogens that rely on antigenic variation for infection, for example Plasmodium and Giardia.
source: Nevertheless, the data indicate that trypanosomes may have evolved a sophisticated mechanism to regulate antigenic variation that entails genetic and signaling processes, and such processes may be conserved in other pathogens that rely on antigenic variation for infection, for example Plasmodium and Giardia, broadening opportunities for drug discovery.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about conservation of mechanisms.

claim: The allosteric regulation of RAP1 by PI(3,4,5)P3 denotes a mechanism for phosphoinositide regulation of telomere silencing.
source: The allosteric regulation of RAP1 by PI(3,4,5)P3 denotes a mechanism for phosphoinositide regulation of telomere silencing.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Telomere silencing is conserved and dependent on RAP1 in most eukaryotes.
source: Given that telomere silencing is conserved and dependent on RAP1 in most eukaryotes, this regulatory system may be present in other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAP1 function across eukaryotes.

claim: The phosphoinositide regulatory system may be present in other eukaryotes.
source: Given that telomere silencing is conserved and dependent on RAP1 in most eukaryotes, this regulatory system may be present in other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about conservation of the regulatory mechanism.

claim: The expressed VSG gene is transcribed by RNA polymerase I (RNAP I) from a compartment outside the nucleolus termed ES body (ESB).
source: The expressed VSG gene is transcribed by RNA polymerase I (RNAP I) from a compartment outside the nucleolus termed ES body (ESB) (Navarro and Gull, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Transcription initiates in all ESs but only elongates through one ES (the active ES).
source: Transcription initiates in all ESs but only elongates through one ES (hereafter called active ES), resulting in VSG monogenic expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ES transcription.

claim: The silencing of ES VSG genes involves its proximity to telomeres.
source: The silencing of ES VSG genes involves its proximity to telomeres (Horn and Cross, 1995; Rudenko et al., 1995) and the telomere-associated factor repressor activator protein 1 (RAP1) (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The silencing of ES VSG genes involves the telomere-associated factor repressor activator protein 1 (RAP1).
source: The silencing of ES VSG genes involves its proximity to telomeres (Horn and Cross, 1995; Rudenko et al., 1995) and the telomere-associated factor repressor activator protein 1 (RAP1) (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 is conserved among eukaryotes.
source: RAP1 is conserved among eukaryotes (Yang et al., 2009; Baur et al., 2001; Myler et al., 2021; Kyrion et al., 1993) and functions in telomere silencing (Yang et al., 2009; Kyrion et al., 1993), telomere end protection (de Lange, 2005; Lototska et al., 2020; Platt et al., 2013), and non-telomeric gene regulation in mammals and yeast (Kyrion et al., 1993; Platt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 functions in telomere silencing.
source: RAP1 is conserved among eukaryotes (Yang et al., 2009; Baur et al., 2001; Myler et al., 2021; Kyrion et al., 1993) and functions in telomere silencing (Yang et al., 2009; Kyrion et al., 1993), telomere end protection (de Lange, 2005; Lototska et al., 2020; Platt et al., 2013), and non-telomeric gene regulation in mammals and yeast (Kyrion et al., 1993; Platt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 functions in telomere end protection.
source: RAP1 is conserved among eukaryotes (Yang et al., 2009; Baur et al., 2001; Myler et al., 2021; Kyrion et al., 1993) and functions in telomere silencing (Yang et al., 2009; Kyrion et al., 1993), telomere end protection (de Lange, 2005; Lototska et al., 2020; Platt et al., 2013), and non-telomeric gene regulation in mammals and yeast (Kyrion et al., 1993; Platt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 functions in non-telomeric gene regulation in mammals and yeast.
source: RAP1 is conserved among eukaryotes (Yang et al., 2009; Baur et al., 2001; Myler et al., 2021; Kyrion et al., 1993) and functions in telomere silencing (Yang et al., 2009; Kyrion et al., 1993), telomere end protection (de Lange, 2005; Lototska et al., 2020; Platt et al., 2013), and non-telomeric gene regulation in mammals and yeast (Kyrion et al., 1993; Platt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Histones and chromatin-modifying enzymes associate with ESs and contribute to their repression.
source: Histones and chromatin-modifying enzymes, such as histone methyltransferase and bromodomain proteins, also associate with ESs and contribute to their repression (Figueiredo and Cross, 2010; Müller et al., 2018; Figueiredo et al., 2008; Schulz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active ES is depleted of nucleosomes.
source: In contrast, the active ES is depleted of nucleosomes (Figueiredo and Cross, 2010) and enriched in proteins that facilitate its transcription, for example VSG exclusion (VEX) 1 and 2 and ES body 1 (ESB1), and processing of the highly abundant VSG mRNAs (Glover et al., 2016; Faria et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active ES is enriched in proteins that facilitate its transcription, for example VEX1 and 2 and ESB1.
source: In contrast, the active ES is depleted of nucleosomes (Figueiredo and Cross, 2010) and enriched in proteins that facilitate its transcription, for example VSG exclusion (VEX) 1 and 2 and ES body 1 (ESB1), and processing of the highly abundant VSG mRNAs (Glover et al., 2016; Faria et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Antigenic variation was thought to occur stochastically.
source: Antigenic variation was thought to occur stochastically (Deitsch et al., 2009) with the DNA break and repair machinery involved in VSG recombination (Boothroyd et al., 2009; Briggs et al., 2018; da Silva et al., 2018; McCulloch and Barry, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The DNA break and repair machinery is involved in VSG recombination.
source: Antigenic variation was thought to occur stochastically (Deitsch et al., 2009) with the DNA break and repair machinery involved in VSG recombination (Boothroyd et al., 2009; Briggs et al., 2018; da Silva et al., 2018; McCulloch and Barry, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphoinositide signaling plays a role in the expression and switching of VSG genes.
source: However, we showed that phosphoinositide signaling plays a role in the expression and switching of VSG genes (Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The phosphoinositide signaling system entails the plasma membrane/cytosolic-localized phosphatidylinositol phosphate 5-kinase (PIP5K) and phospholipase C (PLC).
source: This system entails the plasma membrane/cytosolic-localized phosphatidylinositol phosphate 5-kinase (PIP5K) and phospholipase C (PLC) (Cestari and Stuart, 2015), and the nuclear phosphatidylinositol phosphate 5-phosphatase (PIP5Pase).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The PIP5Pase enzyme interacts with RAP1.
source: The PIP5Pase enzyme interacts with RAP1 (Cestari et al., 2019; Cestari, 2019), and either protein knockdown results in the transcription of all ESs simultaneously (Yang et al., 2009; Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Either PIP5Pase or RAP1 knockdown results in the transcription of all ESs simultaneously.
source: The PIP5Pase enzyme interacts with RAP1 (Cestari et al., 2019; Cestari, 2019), and either protein knockdown results in the transcription of all ESs simultaneously (Yang et al., 2009; Cestari and Stuart, 2015; Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RAP1 and PIP5Pase interact with other nuclear proteins, including nuclear lamina, nucleic acid binding proteins, and protein kinases and phosphatases.
source: RAP1 and PIP5Pase interact with other nuclear proteins, including nuclear lamina, nucleic acid binding proteins, and protein kinases and phosphatases (Cestari et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.
